topic: Expansion of British Power in India
description: During the 18th and 19th centuries, the British East India Company established its supremacy over the Indian subcontinent through a combination of direct military conquests, diplomacy, and expansionist administrative policies.

sections.title: Conquest of Bengal
sections.description: The establishment of political, military, and economic control by the British East India Company over Bengal, which was India's most prosperous province at the time.

key_concepts.explanation: A system introduced by Robert Clive in 1765 in Bengal, where Diwani rights (revenue collection) were held by the Company and Nizamat (administrative and police responsibility) by the Nawab.
An incident in 1756 where Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah confined 146 British prisoners in a very small room at Fort William, resulting in the death of the majority due to suffocation.

historical_events.significance: Robert Clive defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah with the help of Mir Jafar's betrayal. This victory laid the foundational stone of British political power in India.
Hector Munro decisively defeated the combined armies of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah, and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. This established the British as the supreme military power in Northern India.
Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II formally granted the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the British East India Company.

sections.title: Anglo-Mysore Wars
sections.description: A series of four major wars fought between the British East India Company and the Kingdom of Mysore for regional supremacy in South India.

historical_events.significance: Haider Ali successfully defeated the British forces. The war concluded with the Treaty of Madras.
Haider Ali died of cancer during the campaign. The war ended inconclusively with the Treaty of Mangalore, restoring the status quo.
Lord Cornwallis defeated Tipu Sultan. Under the humiliating Treaty of Seringapatam, Tipu had to cede half of his kingdom and pay a heavy war indemnity.
Decisive British victory under Lord Wellesley. Tipu Sultan died defending his capital, and the Hindu Wodeyar Dynasty was restored as a puppet state.

key_associations.extra_info: Planted at Seringapatam inspired by the French Revolution; Tipu also became a member of the French Jacobin Club.

sections.title: Anglo-Maratha Wars
sections.description: Three major conflicts that led to the complete destruction of the Maratha Confederacy and cemented British paramountcy over India.

historical_events.significance: Ended with the Treaty of Salbai, which established a 20-year period of peace between the British and the Marathas.
Triggered by Peshwa Baji Rao II signing the Treaty of Bassein (1802). The British systematically defeated Maratha chiefs like Scindia and Bhonsle.
Final defeat of the Marathas. The title of Peshwa was abolished, and Baji Rao II was pensioned off and exiled to Bithur.

important_facts.fact: Following the Third Anglo-Maratha War, the British installed Pratap Singh, a direct descendant of Chhatrapati Shivaji, as the nominal ruler of the newly created state of Satara.

sections.title: Anglo-Sikh Wars and Annexation of Punjab
sections.description: The rapid decline of the formidable Sikh Empire following Maharaja Ranjit Singh's death, leading to British annexation.

historical_events.significance: Resulted in the defeat of the Sikh Khalsa Army. The Treaty of Lahore imposed heavy war indemnities and reduced the size of the Sikh state.
Resulted in a complete British victory. Lord Dalhousie formally annexed Punjab into the British Empire.

key_associations.extra_info: As part of the Treaty of Lahore following the annexation of Punjab, the young Maharaja was forced to surrender the diamond to Queen Victoria.

sections.title: Expansionist Administrative Policies
sections.description: Strategic, non-military diplomatic doctrines utilized by British Governor-Generals to systematically annex Indian princely states.

key_concepts.explanation: Introduced by Warren Hastings, this policy aimed at creating buffer zones to defend the Company's frontiers against external threats, primarily the Marathas and Afghans.
Introduced by Lord Wellesley. Indian rulers were forced to disband their native armies, maintain a British contingent at their own expense, and accept a British Resident at their court.

An annexation policy heavily used by Lord Dalhousie. If a ruler of a dependent state died without a biological male heir, the state would 'lapse' and be annexed; adopted sons were denied ruling rights.

key_associations.extra_info: The Nizam of Hyderabad was the first Indian ruler to accept the Subsidiary Alliance system.
Satara was the very first princely state to be annexed by the British under the Doctrine of Lapse.
Lord Dalhousie annexed Awadh based on a report by James Outram citing gross maladministration by Nawab Wajid Ali Shah.

important_facts.fact: Lord Dalhousie's ruthless application of the Doctrine of Lapse was one of the primary political catalysts for the Great Revolt of 1857.
